title: 9 Skills the Common Core Doesn’t List but that Employers Want Anyways
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Building on Bill Coplin's 10 Things Employers Want You to Learn in College, Stuart argues that the Common Core, even pared down, omits skills students need for long-term success, and he invites teachers to talk about these with students. The nine skills include motivating yourself, being ethical, managing time, looking presentable, writing legibly, building relationships, selling, politicking wisely and solving problems. For each, he adds his own classroom lens: ownership of learning as the root of self-motivation, faking a reading assignment as a daily ethical choice, procrastination as a self-control issue students should not adopt as identity, and appearance as a real if uncomfortable advantage. He maps several skills onto the KIPP character strengths his team teaches, and describes an ungraded charity: water project in which students design their own campaign to practice identifying and solving real problems. He concludes that no list of standards can capture everything students need, so instruction should be anchored in reasons and long-term flourishing rather than in the standards alone. (Close call: the post spans literacy standards and character, but its argument centers on character, motivation and life skills, so it sits in Practice & Culture.)
points: Stuart argues that students' success hinges on owning their learning, a self-motivation skill the standards never name but teachers fight for every day.
He reframes small classroom moments, like pretending to have read the 'boring book', as ethical choices whose habituation matters for later life.
He tells self-described procrastinators not to make procrastination part of their identity, treating time management as the self-control strength his team teaches.
His ungraded charity: water project, where students plan and launch their own awareness campaigns, is meant to teach problem-solving where 'the test is called life.'
The closing argument is that grounding instruction in long-term student flourishing, rather than in any list of standards, lets teachers teach happier and better.
quotes: This idea of ownership is linked with the skill of motivating yourself. It's just a simple truth: our students won't be successful in college or careers if they don't develop the mentality that this is their life and, therefore, this is their learning.

Again, Coplin treats this less as a moral issue and more as a skill. Students are faced with ethical dilemmas daily; every time they decide to fake their way through an assignment (including pretending that they read the ‘boring book' in English class rather than, you know, actually reading it), they are faced with a decision: will they be honest, or will they be deceptive? The choice that they habituate is important!

These are strong words in my school, where it's completely socially acceptable for a high schooler to wear pajama pants to school. But, as Coplin unabashedly points out, how we look matters, and many of our students are immediately disadvantaged by this truth.

From a character strength perspective, this is social intelligence and interpersonal self-control. Our students need to realize that being a people person isn't an option for most of us; we have to get along with our coworkers if we want to be successful. I will say that the Common Core does mention the ability to collaborate well with anyone (it's in the first Speaking/Listening standard), but this skill is broader and more long-term than that.

In short, it pays to know how to get along with people (hence this skill is closely linked to #6) and how to help people see it your way. While I love the Godfather movies and some of my students do, too, we can't easily make people offers they can't refuse. To help my students learn this, I try to use teachable moments in our discussions to point out what it looks like to make winsome contributions to a conversation or discussion. Also, I seek to relentlessly model politeness in my room, even if we're in the middle of a heated debate on marijuana legalization.

And you already know what happens: some kids hit it out of the park, and some kids do the bare minimum. I try coaching them all during the spare amounts of time I offer during class (after all, this is totally outside of the guaranteed viable curriculum at our school), and I'm happy to see that, even for my kids who fail, they at least get to do something powerful and learn through failing.

The purpose of this post and the two preceding it is to impress upon you, dear teacher who refuses to freak out about the Common Core, that when our instruction is undergirded with reasons, with long-term student flourishing as the ultimate endgame, we can teach happier and better.
